Sunday through Monday morning: A strong low pressure system is 
starting to move inland, with the center of the low crossing over 
the Washington/Oregon border. The main frontal passage looks to take 
place Sunday morning, and will bring widespread rains to the Inland 
Northwest. There are high chances (70 percent and above) for the 
entire forecast area to see at least 0.5 inches of rain. The 
heaviest rainfall looks to be in the Cascades and Wenatchee to the 
Spokane area and northward, alongside the northern Idaho Panhandle. 
While mid and long range models were initially struggling with 
precipitation totals due to the track and speed of the low, 
uncertainty has decreased somewhat now that high-res models can 
capture the event. There is still a good amount of spread in 
precipitation totals, with differences of up to a quarter inch 
between the 25th and 75th percentiles through the areas that are due 
to see the highest rain totals. The bottom line, though, is that the 
majority of the Pacific Northwest will receive 0.5 inches of rain or 
more through Sunday afternoon.  

With the highest rainfall totals expected across much of central, 
north-central, east-central, and northeast Washington, hydrologic 
concerns will increase through the morning and afternoon. Hourly 
rainfall rates through these areas are projected to reach 0.2 to 0.3 
inches, particularly in the morning hours. Excessive runoff from 
these rains could bring a chance for debris and ash flows over burn 
scars in steep terrain, alongside rockslides. Additionally, urban 
areas with poor drainage could see minor flooding, and storm drains 
and ditches may become clogged with debris. For these areas, a Flood 
Watch has been issued from 1 AM Sunday through 8 PM Sunday. A more 
focused Flash Flood Watch has also been issued for the Old Trails 
and Autumn Lane burn scars in Spokane County from 2 AM through 4 PM 
Sunday due to these elevated rainfall rates. Make sure to keep an 
eye on the weather and have ways to receive additional alerts should 
they be necessary. 

Alongside this rainfall, chances for isolated thunderstorms increase 
as the low moves through. There is a 10 to 20 percent chance of 
thunderstorms as the frontal system moves northward through the day. 
For the early part of Sunday, the thunderstorm threat is in the 
southern portion of the forecast area. For Sunday afternoon and 
evening, the threat is for the northern portion of the forecast 
area. Models show CAPE values around 200-400 J/kg, alongside 3-6km 
lapse rates of 7-8 degC/km. With multiple soundings showing very 
saturated mid and low level relative humidities (80 percent and 
above), as well as PWATs 0.5 inches and above, the main risk with 
these thunderstorms will be isolated heavy rainfall rates that could 
contribute to debris flows or flooding. 

Gusty winds will accompany this rainfall as a north-south pressure 
gradient tightens across the northern part of Washington. Wind gusts 
throughout the Waterville Plateau, basin, and Okanogan Valley are 
already gusty ahead of the frontal passage with wind gusts 20-25 mph 
expected through the morning. Wind gusts in the basin will increase 
to 25-30 mph later in the morning with the frontal passage, and will 
relax by Sunday evening. As flow turns westerly after the front has 
passed, an east-west gradient will set up along the Cascades, 
bringing gusty winds to the Cascades, northern mountains, and Idaho 
Panhandle mountains through Monday morning.  

Monday afternoon through Wednesday: As the low moves out of the 
area, broad northwest flow will prevail as heights rise downstream 
of a strong ridge along the Alaskan coast. This will result in 
temperatures starting to warm. On Tuesday, another weaker low moves 
through the area, which will result in light rainfall and isolated 
thunderstorm chances in the northern mountains and in the 
northern ID Panhandle. Elsewhere, expect dry and warming 
conditions. 

Wednesday through Saturday: By Wednesday, 90 percent of clusters 
show high pressure strengthening over the area and persisting 
through the weekend, resulting in a warming and drying trend.
Temperatures will increase back into the mid-70s by Thursday, which 
is a few degrees higher than normal for this time of year. Long 
range guidance indicates temperatures reaching 80 throughout the 
basin by next weekend, showing increasing confidence in a drying and 
warming pattern following the active weekend. /AS
